methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective study of 109 women with apparent early-stage endometrial cancer undergoing robotic hysterectomy/BSO and sentinel lymph node mapping, stratified by BMI group (26 with BMI >= 40, 45 with BMI 30–39, and 38 with BMI < 30) (Abstract). The design is appropriate for feasibility/safety comparisons but is vulnerable to selection bias and confounding (e.g., differences in comorbidity or case complexity across BMI strata) inherent to retrospective single-center series. Statistically, the analysis uses one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc testing for continuous variables and chi-square tests with unadjusted odds ratios for significant categorical outcomes (Section 2.8), which is reasonable for descriptive group comparisons but does not address multivariable adjustment.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual observational cohort study evaluating perioperative outcomes by BMI category, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b (Abstract; Methods 2.1–2.2). The outcomes (conversion to laparotomy, complications, operative time, SLN mapping success) are directly relevant to surgical planning and counseling for patients with class III obesity (Abstract/Results). The work is clinically useful but does not change standards of care on its own given its retrospective design and modest sample size, especially in the BMI >= 40 subgroup (n = 26).

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable checklist for this retrospective cohort study, and the manuscript is explicitly structured with STROBE-like subheadings (Study Design, Participants, Bias, Study Size, Setting, Statistical Analysis) (Sections 2.1–2.8). The statistical methods are clearly stated (ANOVA/Tukey, chi-square, ORs with 95% CIs) and key results are reported with p-values and group-level proportions (e.g., bilateral SLN mapping differences) (Results). Data/code sharing is not described in the blinded text, limiting reproducibility to what is specified in the methods.

novelty_literature.justification: Robotic surgery feasibility in obese endometrial cancer patients has a substantial prior literature, and this study primarily extends it with a class III obesity focus in a single center. The main incremental contribution is quantifying that class III obesity was associated with longer operative time and lower bilateral SLN mapping rates while complications were similar across groups (Abstract/Results). Overall, the novelty is modest and confirmatory.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written, with a structured abstract that provides the cohort size, BMI strata, and key findings with p-values. Methods and results are organized with standard observational-study elements and include concrete outcome definitions and summaries (Sections 2–3). Limitations are acknowledged (Discussion), and the conclusions match the reported data without obvious overclaiming.

key_strengths: Clinically practical question with direct perioperative outcomes for robotic management of early-stage endometrial cancer across BMI strata (Abstract).
Transparent statistical description (ANOVA/Tukey; chi-square; ORs/95% CIs) and clear reporting of key differences such as operative time and bilateral SLN mapping rates (Methods 2.8; Results).
Explicit discussion of limitations including retrospective single-center design and potential selection effects (Discussion/Conclusions).
key_concerns: Retrospective single-center design with likely residual confounding; group comparisons are largely unadjusted (Methods 2.8).
Small class III obesity subgroup (n = 26) and low event counts limit power to detect complication differences and to support strong equivalence claims (Abstract/Results).
Generalizability may be limited to experienced centers using similar robotic and SLN protocols (Setting in Abstract).
chief_reviewer.rationale: A well-reported single-center retrospective cohort with clinically useful, mostly confirmatory findings; it fits a Tier 3 audience and would likely be publishable after minor revisions emphasizing confounding and power limits.
